- [Nanjing Maritime Court] emphasized refining the trial process and guaranteeing fair and efficient trial of cases [d0].  
- It formulated trial guidelines to standardize judicial behavior and unify judgment standards [d0].  
- It won trust of the international community in China’s maritime justice through professional handling of an international shipbuilding contract case [d0].  
- [Guangzhou Maritime Court] highlighted “successful practice to deliver quality cases” by listing cases selected by [Supreme People’s Court] as typical or excellent cases [d3].  
- It also presented quantitative trial and enforcement data, such as cases accepted/closed and enforcement rates [d3].

Nanjing Maritime Court organized professional judge teams, an assessment mechanism, and a research pool to conduct in-depth discussions on professional cases [d1]. It resolved an international shipbuilding contract dispute through Internet mediation in 27 days, reflecting trust in its professional judicial ability and optimized judicial environment [d1]. Guangzhou Maritime Court presented typical cases and suggestions on crew labor contracts, FOB carriage, administrative agreements, concurrent torts, seafarer wages, and limitation of liability funds [d4,d7].

- [Nanjing Maritime Court] emphasized “standardized law enforcement” in a ship-arrest case and created appraisal, guarantee, and cooperative mechanisms to improve implementation efficiency and protect parties’ rights [d2].
- [Nanjing Maritime Court] promoted people-centered justice and one-stop fishery dispute resolution for livelihood cases [d2].
- [Guangzhou Maritime Court]’s 2020 report lists “Successful practice to deliver quality cases” among its general trial information/achievements [d2].
- [Guangzhou Maritime Court] uses case studies to identify risks and provide solutions/suggestions to shipping market participants and authorities [d2].
- [Guangzhou Maritime Court] supplied enforcement case analyses on ship arrest/auction [d8].

Relevant facts: [Phidias] introduces [meta-ControlNet] to dynamically modulate conditioning strength when the [3D reference] conflicts with the [concept image], based on their similarity [d0]. It treats the reference as auxiliary guidance, not requiring precise alignment, addressing the [Misalignment Dilemma] where image-reference discrepancy causes generation conflicts [d0]. [meta-ControlNet] uses [Multi-Scale Alignment Features], [Adaptive Control Signal], [Meta-Controller], [Zero Convs], and [Base ControlNet] with encoders for [Concept Image] and [3D Reference CCM] [d0]. These designs help [Phidias] use misaligned references adaptively and improve generalization [d0]. [d3] mentions cosine similarity for retrieval, not explicitly for [meta-ControlNet] gradients.

[Phidias] uses [Meta-ControlNet] for adaptive control of conditioning strength when a [3D reference] misaligns with a [concept image] [d1]. A [meta-controller] takes a pair of the [concept image] and front-view [reference CCM], producing [multi-scale alignment features] and [meta-signals] based on their similarities; final [adaptive control signals] combine base and meta signals [d1]. This modulates how strongly reference CCMs condition diffusion, reducing conflicts from misaligned references [d1]. [Dynamic Reference Routing] lowers reference resolution at high noise and increases it at lower noise to balance global structure and local details [d1]. [Self-reference augmentation] and curriculum training expose the model to misaligned references, improving generalization [d1].

Relevant facts:
- [d2] Phidias includes meta-ControlNet, which dynamically modulates the conditioning strength of a 3D reference model to handle varying similarity among retrieved references.
- [d2] Without meta-ControlNet, a base model trained with retrieved references often ignores the reference and fails to follow its shape pattern because similarity variation confuses the diffusion model.
- [d2] Adding meta-ControlNet improves PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS, CLIP-P/I, and CD over the base model.
- [d2] Dynamic Reference Routing alleviates local conflicts between reference and concept image; Self-Reference Augmentation keeps outputs faithful to the concept image when references are misaligned.
- [d2] Phidias remains robust to random references and generalizes across similarity levels.

- [d0] Dupixent (dupilumab) is a fully human monoclonal antibody inhibiting IL4/IL13 signaling.  
- [d0] Dupixent has regulatory approvals in more than 60 countries for indications including EoE, CSU, COPD, asthma, atopic dermatitis, CRSwNP, and prurigo nodularis.  
- [d0] BP and CPUO safety/efficacy are under clinical investigation and not evaluated by any regulatory authority; the ADEPT BP pivotal study met endpoints, supporting future submissions.  
- [d3] CHMP recommended EU expanded approval for EoE in children aged 1–11 years, weighing at least 15 kg, inadequately controlled, intolerant, or not candidates for conventional therapy; not yet approved.  
- [d3] EoE is a chronic, progressive disease associated with type-2 inflammation.  
- [d6] Regeneron forward-looking statements mention potential Dupixent indications including COPD, CPUO, and BP.

- FDA approved Dupixent for adults with inadequately controlled COPD and an eosinophilic phenotype; approval was based on phase 3 BOREAS and NOTUS efficacy/safety data [d7].
- Dupixent has regulatory approvals in more than 60 countries for indications including EoE, chronic spontaneous urticaria, and COPD [d7,d4].
- Dupixent is a fully human monoclonal antibody inhibiting IL-4 and IL-13 pathways [d7,d4].
- Dupilumab is in phase 3 studies for chronic pruritus of unknown origin and bullous pemphigoid; these uses are not fully evaluated [d7,d4,d1].
- EoE can severely impact a child’s ability to eat; a CHMP opinion relates to potential EU approval for pediatric EoE aged 1–11 [d4].

[Sanofi/Regeneron press release] [Dupixent] COPD approval in China was based on [BOREAS] and [NOTUS] phase 3 studies showing reduced exacerbations, improved lung function, and health-related quality of life [d5]. [Dupixent] for COPD is approved in more than 30 countries, including 27 EU countries; US and Japan submissions are under review [d5]. [Dupixent] has approvals in more than 60 countries for one or more indications, including atopic dermatitis, asthma, chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps, eosinophilic esophagitis, prurigo nodularis, CSU, and COPD [d2,d5]. [Dupixent] inhibits IL-4/IL-13 signaling [d2,d5]. Phase 3 studies include chronic pruritus of unknown origin and bullous pemphigoid [d2,d5,d8]. [CSU] approval in Japan; US resubmission planned [d2].

The Law Reform (Marriage and Divorce) Act 1976 (LRA) repealed non-Muslim marriage/divorce statutes, regulated customary marriages, abolished polygamy, required registration, and made conciliation a precondition to divorce [d0]. Rural confusion and low legal literacy required campaigns [d0]. Malaysia has a dual system: non-Muslims are subject to secular law/courts; Muslims to secular and Shari’a law, with Shari’a administered by 13 states and separate interpretations [d3]. Muslim family law is state-controlled; enactments vary from the federal IFLA model [d6]. Muslim women face unequal marriage rights (wali), unequal divorce (talaq by men; limited grounds for women), and male-only polygamy with court permission [d6]. No shard evidence on harta sepencarian.

State Islamic Family Law enactments were based on a model but modified, producing non-uniform Islamic family law; some enactments’ polygamy controls facilitate circumvention [d1]. New enactments codified Shari’a and spelled out rights, improving legal literacy, though some kadis initially ignored statutory polygamy controls [d1]. Kelantan’s Section 19 requires court permission for polygamy but did not require informing wives and accepted unsupported declarations/low income [d1]. Section 35 requires talaq applications and payment of najkah edah, mutaah, mas kahwin, and harta sepencarian [d1]. Wife-initiated divorce was weakly implemented; kadis/hakam often pushed women to costly kholo [d1]. Malaysia has dual civil/Shari’a courts; Shari’a courts handle Muslim personal law, and the 1988 amendment limits civil-court jurisdiction/appeal [d4]. Article 8(5) permits discrimination in personal law [d7].

- LRA 1976 (Act 164) governs non-Muslim marriages; s3 excludes Muslims/Islamic-law marriages [d5].
- s51 permits civil divorce after one spouse converts to Islam, but converted spouse cannot file in civil court; often husband converts, leaving wife without maintenance/ancillary relief; possible dual civil/Shari’a divorces [d5].
- Shari’a courts have jurisdiction only over Muslims and belong to State jurisdiction; civil courts lack Shari’a jurisdiction [d5].
- CEDAW Committee notes dual civil/multiple Syariah systems cause continuing discrimination against women in marriage/family; Malaysia reserved CEDAW Art 16 [d8].
- Muslim women’s maintenance is limited to iddah (~3 months), shorter than civil courts [d8].
- harta sepencarian, rooted in adat and administered by Shari’a courts, gives property shares but women face proof, legal aid, and access barriers [d2].
- Islamic divorce includes talaq, khul’, ta’liq, faskh [d8].
